import Mathlib.Data.Nat.Notation

/-!
---
title: Types
type: definition
---
*Types* are the expressions generated by the grammar
$$
A \;::=\; 1 \;\mid\; A \times A \;\mid\; A + A \;\mid\; A^* .
$$
A type denotes a set: $1$ is a one-element set, $A \times B$ is the Cartesian product,
$A + B$ is the disjoint union, and $A^*$ is the set of finite lists over $A$.

Elements of types are represented as strings over the eight-letter alphabet
$$
\mathbb{8} = \{\, (\,,\ )\,,\ [\,,\ ]\,,\ \texttt{,}\,,\ 1,\ \mathsf{Left},\ \mathsf{Right} \,\}:
$$
the element of $1$ is written $1$, an element of $A + B$ is written $\mathsf{Left}\,a$ or
$\mathsf{Right}\,b$, a pair is written $(a,b)$ and a list is written $[a_1,\ldots,a_n]$.

A type is a *finite alphabet* if it has the form $1 + \cdots + 1$. We write
$\overline{n+1}$ for the finite alphabet with $n+1$ letters, bracketed to the right.

# Formalization notes

The finite alphabet with $n+1$ letters is `Ty.finAlph n`, defined as `1` for $n = 0$ and
as `1 + finAlph n` otherwise. A type is a finite alphabet (`Ty.IsFinAlph`) if it is equal
to one of these; the paper does not fix a bracketing of the sum, and any bracketing is
isomorphic to the right-bracketed one.

`Ty.someElem` picks a canonical element of every type; it shows that every type is
nonempty and is used to state the decision procedure of Corollary 2.8.
-/

namespace Lax149335.Types

/-- Types: the unit type `1`, products `A × B`, co-products `A + B` and lists `A*`. -/
inductive Ty : Type
  | unit : Ty
  | prod : Ty → Ty → Ty
  | sum : Ty → Ty → Ty
  | list : Ty → Ty
  deriving DecidableEq, Repr

namespace Ty

/-- Notation `A ⊗ B` for the product type. -/
infixl:70 " ⊗ " => Ty.prod
/-- Notation `A ⊕' B` for the co-product type. -/
infixl:65 " ⊕' " => Ty.sum
/-- Notation `A⋆` for the list type. -/
postfix:max "⋆" => Ty.list

/-- The set denoted by a type. -/
def den : Ty → Type
  | .unit => Unit
  | .prod A B => den A × den B
  | .sum A B => den A ⊕ den B
  | .list A => List (den A)

/-- Notation `⟦A⟧` for the set denoted by a type. -/
notation "⟦" A "⟧" => Ty.den A

/-- The eight-letter alphabet used to represent elements of types as strings. -/
inductive Sym : Type
  | lpar | rpar | lbrack | rbrack | comma | one | left | right
  deriving DecidableEq, Repr

/-- The string representing an element of a type: `1`, `Left a`, `Right b`, `(a,b)` and
`[a₁,…,aₙ]`. -/
def repr : (A : Ty) → ⟦A⟧ → List Sym
  | .unit, _ => [Sym.one]
  | .prod A B, (a, b) => Sym.lpar :: (repr A a ++ Sym.comma :: repr B b ++ [Sym.rpar])
  | .sum A _, .inl a => Sym.left :: repr A a
  | .sum _ B, .inr b => Sym.right :: repr B b
  | .list A, l =>
      Sym.lbrack :: ((l.map (repr A)).intersperse [Sym.comma]).flatten ++ [Sym.rbrack]

/-- A canonical element of every type. -/
def someElem : (A : Ty) → ⟦A⟧
  | .unit => ()
  | .prod A B => (someElem A, someElem B)
  | .sum A _ => .inl (someElem A)
  | .list _ => []

/-- The finite alphabet `1 + (1 + ⋯ + 1)` with `n + 1` letters. -/
def finAlph : ℕ → Ty
  | 0 => Ty.unit
  | (n + 1) => Ty.sum Ty.unit (finAlph n)

/-- A type is a finite alphabet if it has the form `1 + ⋯ + 1`. -/
def IsFinAlph (A : Ty) : Prop := ∃ n : ℕ, A = finAlph n

end Ty

end Lax149335.Types

**Lemma 5.2 (Concatenation with values).** For terms $f : A \to B^*$ and
$g : A' \to B^*$ and list values $w, v : 1 \to B^*$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
(f \cdot w) \cdot v &\equiv f \cdot (w \cdot v), &
w \cdot (v \cdot f) &\equiv (w \cdot v) \cdot f, &
f \cdot [\,] &\equiv f \equiv [\,] \cdot f, \\
(w \cdot f) \cdot v &\equiv w \cdot (f \cdot v), &
(f \cdot w) \odot g &\equiv f \odot (w \cdot g).
\end{aligned}
$$

/-- **Lemma 5.2.** The associativity and unit laws for concatenation with values. -/
axiom value_assoc {A A' B : Ty} (f : Term A B⋆) (g : Term A' B⋆) (w v : Value B⋆) :

    (dotR (dotL w f) v ≡ₜ dotL w (dotR f v)) ∧
    (fdot (dotR f w) g ≡ₜ fdot f (dotL w g))

end Lax149335.ValueConcatenation

import Lax149335.EquationalTheory

/-!
---
title: Normalisation of values
type: lemma
---
**Lemma 5.3 (Normalisation of values).** Every value $1 \to A$ is provably equivalent to a
value built from the identity on $1$ using the following constructors: $v \mathbin{;}
\mathsf{Left}$ and $v \mathbin{;} \mathsf{Right}$ for values of co-products, $(v, w)$ for
values of products, and $v \cdot w$, $[v]$ and $[\,]$ for values of list types.
-/

namespace Lax149335.ValueNormalisation

open Lax149335.Types Lax149335.Terms Lax149335.Terms.Term Lax149335.DerivedTerms
  Lax149335.DerivedTerms.Term Lax149335.EquationalTheory

/-- Values in normal form. -/
inductive NormalValue : {A : Ty} → Value A → Prop
  /-- The identity on the unit type. -/
  | id : NormalValue (Term.id Ty.unit)
  /-- A co-product value `v; Left`. -/
  | inl {A B : Ty} {v : Value A} : NormalValue v → NormalValue (v ⨟ Term.inl A B)
  /-- A co-product value `v; Right`. -/
  | inr {A B : Ty} {v : Value B} : NormalValue v → NormalValue (v ⨟ Term.inr A B)
  /-- A product value `(v, w)`. -/
  | pair {A B : Ty} {v : Value A} {w : Value B} :
      NormalValue v → NormalValue w → NormalValue (pairR v w)
  /-- The concatenation `v · w` of two list values. -/
  | dot {A : Ty} {v w : Value A⋆} : NormalValue v → NormalValue w → NormalValue (dotL v w)
  /-- A singleton list value `[v]`. -/
  | sing {A : Ty} {v : Value A} : NormalValue v → NormalValue (sing v)
  /-- The empty list value `[]`. -/
  | nil {A : Ty} : NormalValue (nilT A)

/-- **Lemma 5.3.** Every value is provably equivalent to a value in normal form. -/
axiom normalisation_of_values {A : Ty} (v : Value A) : ∃ u : Value A, NormalValue u ∧ v ≡ₜ u

end Lax149335.ValueNormalisation

proofs.description: Compose with the one-sided inverse and use the category axioms.
Compare the outputs on inputs that differ by one element in a single list component.

Reduce to binary string outputs with the encoding of Lemma 5.6 and Lemma 5.5. Factorise the
two terms as a common lift followed by drops (Lemmas 7.4 and 7.2). The two drops have the
same denotation, so they are provably equivalent by Lemma 7.3 and Lemma 6.1, and the common
lift is cancelled with Lemma 5.5.

The completeness rule and the conjugacy rule are proved together by induction on the nesting
depth of lists in the input type. The completeness rule follows the proof of Theorem 2.6.
For the conjugacy rule with a nonempty value `w` of length `k`, Lemmas 6.4 and 6.5 reduce to
co-pairings of `k`-guarded nonempty terms. After grouping the list into bundles of size at
least `k` with the bundle lemma (Lemma 6.7), the bundled terms become syntactically
`w`-conjugate, by the induction hypothesis, and Lemma 6.2 applies. The bundle isomorphism is
cancelled with Lemma 5.5.

For binary strings and bundles of size two, the window axiom provides the inverse of the
concatenation map. Every type is a retract of the binary strings, by Lemma 5.6, and
concatenation maps are natural, which gives bundles of size two for every type. Bundles of
bundles multiply the bundle sizes, which gives all powers of two.

Soundness of the rules is checked rule by rule. Completeness is proved by induction on the
input type: the rules for moving constants bring a term into a normal form determined by the
input type, and the induction steps for products and lists use Levi's lemma, the latter
together with the conjugacy rule.

Both sides factor through the list of pairs `(h(a), w)`; the two factorisations are related
by shifting the brackets of a list of pairs whose first components are values (the *shift
ones* lemma) and naturality of `shiftL`.

By induction on the input type: over a co-product the two summands are compared, over a
product each component is compared with the other one fixed, and over a list type the empty
list and the singleton lists are compared; the last two cases are applications of Levi's
lemma.

By a syntactic analysis of drops: drops with co-product, product and list codomains are
normalised, the normal forms of two drops are brought to a common shape by a common lift,
and a drop of that shape into the lists over a finite alphabet is provably equivalent to a
simple rational term.

By induction on the lift. The combinators and all atomic lifts except `shift` and `split`
are straightforward; the cases of `shift` and `split` are the shift exchange and the split
exchange lemmas of the appendix.

A type is first encoded injectively into strings over a finite alphabet, by induction on the
type, and the finite alphabet is then encoded into binary strings by blocks of a fixed
length that is a power of two, using the injectivity half of the bundle lemma.

Soundness is checked axiom by axiom against the denotational semantics. For completeness,
let `f, g : A → B` have the same denotation. Postcomposing with the injective binary
encoding `enc : B → 2*` of Lemma 5.6, Theorem 7.7 (provable simplification) gives a surjective
term `π` such that `π ; f ; enc` and `π ; g ; enc` are provably equivalent to simple
rational terms. These have the same denotation, so they are provably equivalent by
Lemma 6.1, and `π` and `enc` are cancelled with Lemma 5.5.

The empty case contributes nothing to the homomorphism, by the axioms about empty lists
(Axioms 10 and 14).

By induction on the term. The atomic terms are factorised directly, the functoriality
combinators preserve factorisations, and for a composition the inner drop-lift is turned
into a lift-drop by the exchange lemma.

By induction on the lift. The combinators are handled by functoriality, and each atomic lift
has a drop inverse by the isomorphism axioms; for `split` the inverse is the concatenation
map `unsplit`, and for `shift` it is `⟨[], unshift⟩`.

Every term composed with the value representing an element of a type is provably equivalent
to the value representing the image of that element; the lemma is the special case of a
value applied to the unique element of `1`.

The grouplift-drop factorisation of the appendix gives a group-lift `α : A → C` with a
one-sided inverse `α⁻¹`, i.e. `α ; α⁻¹ ≡ id`, such that `α⁻¹ ; f` and `α⁻¹ ; g` are provably
equivalent to drops. By Lemma 7.3 there is a lift `σ : C → B` with inverse `σ⁻¹` such that
`σ⁻¹` composed with these drops gives simple rational terms. The term `π = σ⁻¹ ; α⁻¹` is
surjective, since `(α ; σ) ; π ≡ id`.

By Theorem 7.7 (provable simplification), there is a surjective term `π` after which both
terms are provably equivalent to simple rational terms of the compositional syntax. By
soundness, the denotation of `π` is surjective, and the denotations of the two compositions
are those of simple rational terms of the compositional syntax, which are represented by
simple rational terms of Definition 2.5.

Each law is derived from the monoid axioms for `binconcat` (Axiom 10) and the coherence laws
for products, which in turn follow from Mac Lane's pentagon and triangle.

By value extraction, there is an isomorphism after which both terms are co-pairings of
`k`-guarded terms; the conclusion is transported back along this isomorphism.

The input type is split into the summands on which both terms produce the empty list and the
remaining ones; the former are removed with Claim 6.6.
